title: So, what is the cloud?
summary: Understand what happens behind the scenes when you use an app, save a file, or launch a server.
body: Cloud computing is on-demand access to computing resources over the internet. Instead of buying and maintaining your own hardware, you rent what you need from a provider and scale it as demand changes.
tryThis: Name one app you use that stores or processes your data in the cloud.

quiz.question: How do users typically access cloud resources?
options: Only from a local hard drive
quiz.explanation: Cloud services are typically reached over a network, commonly the internet.

quiz.question: What does cloud computing let you do instead of buying all your own hardware?
options: Store every file on your device
quiz.explanation: Cloud customers provision resources from a provider as needed.

quiz.question: Why is on-demand scaling useful?
options: Resources can better match changing demand
It removes the need to monitor services
It guarantees every service is free
quiz.explanation: Scaling lets capacity change as workload demand changes.

title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
summary: Three service models, one useful question: how much of the stack do you want to manage?
body: IaaS rents building blocks like virtual machines. PaaS adds a managed environment for deploying apps. SaaS gives you a finished application. As you move from IaaS to SaaS, the provider manages more of the underlying stack.
tryThis: Sort email hosting, a virtual machine, and a managed app platform into these three models.

quiz.question: Which model provides a finished application?
quiz.explanation: SaaS is software delivered as a ready-to-use service.

quiz.question: In which model does the customer manage the most underlying software layers?
quiz.explanation: IaaS gives customers virtualized infrastructure and more responsibility for its software stack.

quiz.question: Moving from IaaS toward SaaS generally means:
options: The provider manages more of the stack
The customer owns more physical servers
quiz.explanation: Higher-level managed services transfer more operational responsibility to the provider.

title: Public, private, and hybrid cloud
summary: Learn the main deployment approaches and why organizations sometimes combine them.
body: Public cloud resources are delivered by a provider over shared infrastructure. A private cloud is dedicated to one organization. Hybrid cloud connects cloud environments with private infrastructure; multi-cloud uses services from more than one provider.
tryThis: Consider which data, compliance, or existing-system requirements might influence a deployment choice.

quiz.question: What is characteristic of public cloud?
options: A provider delivers resources over shared infrastructure
Every customer owns a separate data center
It cannot connect to private infrastructure
quiz.explanation: Public cloud services are provided over infrastructure shared across customers.

quiz.question: What does a hybrid cloud connect?
quiz.explanation: Hybrid cloud combines cloud resources with private infrastructure.

quiz.question: What does multi-cloud mean?
options: Using services from more than one cloud provider
Using several availability zones from one provider
quiz.explanation: Multi-cloud describes using services from multiple providers.

title: Choosing a cloud provider
summary: A grounded way to compare AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud beyond the brand names.
body: All three offer global infrastructure and broad service catalogs. Compare the services your workload actually needs, your team's existing skills, regional availability, support, and the total cost of a realistic design.
tryThis: Pick a workload and write down its must-haves before comparing providers.

quiz.question: What is a useful basis for comparing cloud providers?
options: Workload needs, team skills, regions, support, and cost
The number of products in a catalog
quiz.explanation: Provider selection should reflect workload and organization requirements.

quiz.question: Why can regional availability matter?
options: It affects placement, latency, and data location choices
quiz.explanation: Regions affect where services run and can influence latency and compliance.

quiz.question: Which statement about major cloud providers is most accurate?
options: The best fit depends on the workload and team
One provider is always best for every workload
Providers offer identical services and pricing
quiz.explanation: Different workload and team requirements make provider fit contextual.

title: Regions, networks, and resilience
summary: See how cloud locations and virtual networks connect applications and help keep them available.
body: A region is a geographic area; availability zones are isolated locations within it. Virtual networks let you define how cloud resources communicate. Using multiple zones can reduce the impact of a single-zone outage, while multi-region designs can address larger disruptions and latency.
tryThis: Trace how a user request reaches an application and its data store.

quiz.question: What is a cloud region?
options: A geographic area containing cloud locations
quiz.explanation: A region is a geographic area where a provider operates cloud infrastructure.

quiz.question: What is an availability zone?
options: An isolated location within a region
quiz.explanation: Availability zones are isolated locations within a region.

quiz.question: What do virtual networks help define?
options: Which code editor a team uses
quiz.explanation: Virtual networks define connectivity and traffic paths between cloud resources.

title: Compute, storage, and databases
summary: Get familiar with the building blocks behind most cloud applications and when each is useful.
body: Compute runs application code on virtual machines, containers, or serverless functions. Object storage holds files and backups; block storage attaches disks to machines. Relational databases organize structured records, while NoSQL databases support other data models and access patterns.
tryThis: Match an image archive, a web server, and a customer order table to suitable cloud services.

quiz.question: What does compute do?
quiz.explanation: Compute services provide processing resources for application code.

quiz.question: Which storage type is commonly used for files and backups?
quiz.explanation: Object storage is commonly used for files, media, and backup data.

quiz.question: Relational databases are designed around:
quiz.explanation: Relational databases organize structured data into related tables.

title: Containers and serverless
summary: Compare two ways to package and run applications without managing every server directly.
body: A container packages an application with its dependencies so it behaves consistently across environments. Serverless services run code or applications without requiring you to manage the underlying servers, though you still configure and monitor the service. Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale and is not necessary for every app.
tryThis: Compare the operational control you need with the amount of infrastructure you want to manage.

quiz.question: What does a container package?
quiz.explanation: Containers package an application with dependencies for consistent execution.

quiz.question: With serverless, who manages the underlying servers?
quiz.explanation: The provider manages the underlying servers, while customers still configure and monitor their services.

quiz.question: What does Kubernetes primarily do?
quiz.explanation: Kubernetes automates deployment and operation of containerized workloads.

title: Cloud security and shared responsibility
summary: Understand what providers secure, what you still own, and how access should be granted.
body: Providers secure the underlying cloud infrastructure, while customers remain responsible for their data, identities, access settings, and workloads. The exact split depends on the service. Use identity and access management to give each person or application only the permissions it needs, and protect data with encryption and backups.
tryThis: Review who can access a test project and remove permissions that are not needed.

quiz.question: In shared responsibility, what does the customer remain responsible for?
options: Data, identities, access settings, and workloads
quiz.explanation: Customers retain responsibility for their data, identities, configurations, and workloads.

quiz.question: What does least privilege mean?
options: Grant only the access a person or service needs
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits permissions to what is needed for a task.

quiz.question: Why encrypt cloud data?
options: To help protect it from unauthorized access
quiz.explanation: Encryption helps protect data confidentiality at rest and in transit.

title: Monitoring, backups, and recovery
summary: Plan how to spot problems, restore important data, and recover from service interruptions.
body: Monitoring tracks signals such as availability, latency, and errors so teams can investigate issues. Backups create recoverable copies of data; disaster recovery describes how services are restored after a major disruption. Test restores regularly because an untested backup may not meet recovery needs.
tryThis: Decide how much data loss and downtime a simple project could tolerate.

quiz.question: What can monitoring help teams detect?
quiz.explanation: Monitoring tracks service signals such as availability, latency, and errors.

quiz.question: Why should teams test backup restores?
options: To verify data can actually be recovered
To increase the size of a bill
quiz.explanation: A backup is useful only if it can be restored when needed.

quiz.question: What does disaster recovery planning address?
options: Restoring services after a major disruption
quiz.explanation: Disaster recovery plans how services and data are restored after serious incidents.

title: Keep cloud costs in view
summary: Build a few sensible habits for visibility before your first bill becomes a surprise.
body: Tag resources by owner or project, set budget alerts, review usage regularly, and remove resources you no longer need. Budgets notify you about spend; they do not automatically cap it, so pair alerts with clear ownership.
tryThis: Set a small test budget and an alert before experimenting with paid services.

quiz.question: Do budget alerts automatically cap cloud spending?
options: No, they notify you about spending
quiz.explanation: Budget alerts are notifications, not automatic spending limits.

quiz.question: Why tag cloud resources?
quiz.explanation: Tags help organize usage and assign costs to teams or projects.

quiz.question: What is a sensible way to reduce avoidable costs?
options: Review usage and remove idle resources
quiz.explanation: Regular usage reviews can reveal resources that are no longer needed.
